sources.title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids — summary
sources.text: Flame spread and extinction over realistic solid fuels (cotton-fiberglass fabric, PMMA in several geometries, Nomex) in low-speed forced flow aboard the ISS. Built to bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening method and real microgravity flammability, and to test an inert gaseous extinguishing agent.

sources.title: Microgravity and 1-g rankings of materials can disagree
sources.text: In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone samples (0.27–1.03 mm) had a burn length of about 0 in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while 2 of the 4 matching 1-g reference burns were complete. Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). Limitation: One test per configuration; single flow speed and near-normal O2.

sources.title: Scale matters: only SAFFIRE burned spacecraft-size samples
sources.text: SAFFIRE-I and -III burned ~0.4 m × 0.94 m fabric samples in uncrewed Cygnus vehicles, with O2/CO2, pressure, temperature and flame-growth measurements — the only realistic-scale fire data in PSI. Limitation: Two samples per mission, one material (SIBAL).

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations are free text; flow units to be confirmed in the BASS-II documentation; flame-spread rates are in the raw video data.

sources.title: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative
sources.text: Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better in microgravity than in normal gravity. Limitation: Specific materials and geometries; flow and O2 per test partly only in raw files for BASS.

top_passage.text: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions.

top_passage.text: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.

top_passage.text: The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing.
